title: Linear Mechanisms for Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Vision Language Models

response.summary: The paper proposes that VLMs bind approximately linear spatial/temporal “IDs” to object-token activations, supporting this with activation swapping, extracted directions, steering, diagnostics, and a small fine-tuning study. The idea is interesting and potentially useful, but the supplied evidence does not yet justify the strong claim that these IDs constitute the causal mechanism of spatiotemporal reasoning.
strengths: A novel, coherent mechanistic hypothesis connects cross-modal information transfer to linear representations on object tokens (pp. 3–5).
The study combines observational structure with interventions and reports broad spatial steering across 11 VLMs rather than relying on probing alone (pp. 5–6).
The proposed representations have promising applications to failure analysis, training, and video models (pp. 7–10).
weaknesses: Steering mainly establishes sufficiency, not that the extracted IDs are the naturally used mechanism: interventions are very large (alpha=5), selected to reverse beliefs, and the noise control itself swaps 29.5% of predictions. Controls matched to the spatial subspace, shuffled locations, and intervention geometry are missing (pp. 5–6).

Several diagnostic conclusions are underidentified. Pixel masking affects the complete pipeline and cannot localize failure to the vision encoder; moreover, a null masking result (p=0.53) does not establish that LLaMA fails during cross-modal integration (pp. 7–9).

Key evidence is insufficiently documented or replicated: the supplied PDF contains no appendices despite repeatedly deferring experimental details and multi-model results to them; the temporal analysis is mostly qualitative/noisy, and the fine-tuning gain lacks seeds, uncertainty, and stronger supervision controls (pp. 9–10).
response.score_rationale: The work has good novelty and unusually broad exploratory experiments, but causal claims are overstated relative to the controls, and central implementation details and claimed appendices are absent from the supplied manuscript. I therefore place it marginally below acceptance, with some uncertainty because the missing appendices might address part of these concerns.

response.summary: The paper proposes “spatiotemporal IDs”: approximately linear location components bound to object-token activations in VLMs. Activation swapping, extracted directions, and steering provide suggestive evidence that intermediate object-token representations carry causally relevant spatial information, with extensions to diagnostics, training, and video. However, the evidence does not yet establish that these directions constitute the claimed underlying reasoning mechanism rather than manipulable correlates, and several decisive experimental details and controls are unavailable or weak.
strengths: The object-token binding hypothesis is intuitive and moderately novel as a mechanistic account connecting visual localization to language-space reasoning (pp. 1–5).

The paper uses interventions rather than probes alone and evaluates adversarial steering across 11 image VLMs; spatial-ID steering swaps beliefs substantially more often than norm-matched noise (pp. 5–7).
The work explores useful consequences beyond the core observation, including failure diagnosis, auxiliary supervision, and an analogous temporal effect in video models (pp. 7–10).
weaknesses: The causal interpretation is overstated: adding large, grid-searched perturbations (alpha=5) can control logits without showing that the model naturally uses the same linear variable as its reasoning mechanism; even norm-matched noise swaps 29.5% of beliefs, and key intervention results lack stronger causal controls such as matched non-spatial directions, dose-response analyses, or mediation/completeness tests (pp. 5–7).

Important empirical support is deferred to appendices that are not present in the supplied manuscript, including extraction invariance, counterfactuals, axis orthogonality, low-rank-fit details, per-model results, and implementation specifics. Main-text plots often show only one model and do not clearly report sample sizes, uncertainty, seeds, or multiple-testing treatment (pp. 3–6, 10–14).

The downstream claims are under-supported: masking an input cannot cleanly localize errors to the vision encoder versus cross-modal integration, while the training result uses one 2B model, apparently differing initial losses, no variance across runs, and a synthetic training setup closely related to ID extraction (pp. 7–9).
response.score_rationale: This is a promising and potentially useful interpretability direction with broad model coverage and genuine intervention-based evidence. Nevertheless, central mechanistic and architectural-localization claims exceed what the presented controls justify, and missing appendix material prevents verification of several decisive robustness claims. I therefore place it marginally below acceptance, with some uncertainty because the omitted details could materially strengthen the work.

response.summary: The paper proposes that VLMs bind approximately linear spatial or temporal “IDs” to object-token activations and supports this with activation swapping, steering, diagnostics, and a small supervised-training study. The mechanism is interesting and potentially useful, but the evidence does not yet justify the broad causal and architectural conclusions.
strengths: A novel, intuitive hypothesis connects cross-modal information transfer with linear binding mechanisms, supported by layer-localized swapping effects (pp. 3–5).
Interventions span 11 image VLMs and include norm-matched random-noise controls; the reported targeted steering effect is substantial (pp. 2, 5–7).
The paper explores useful downstream implications—failure diagnosis, spatial supervision, and temporal extension—rather than stopping at probing (pp. 7–10).
weaknesses: Causal claims are overstated: adding large, tuned perturbations (α=5) shows controllability but not that the extracted directions constitute the naturally used mechanism. The 29.5% noise swap rate is high, and stronger matched-subspace, dose-response, token, and semantic controls are missing (pp. 5–7).

Several diagnostic conclusions are not identified by the experiments. End-to-end sensitivity to pixel masking cannot cleanly separate vision-encoder failures from cross-modal integration, and absence of a masking difference does not establish that LLaMA fails during integration (pp. 7–9).

Evidence and reproducibility are incomplete in the supplied manuscript: repeatedly cited appendices and model-wise details are absent; the finetuning result uses one model and one apparent run without uncertainty, with mismatched step-0 losses, while the temporal evidence is largely one-model summary plots (pp. 9–10).
response.score_rationale: The central idea is promising and the multi-model interventions provide meaningful evidence for a linear spatial signal. However, missing appendices, insufficient causal controls, underdetermined failure localization, and limited training/temporal validation leave the main mechanistic and practical claims below the acceptance bar. I am moderately confident, though fuller appendices could resolve some uncertainty.

response.summary: The paper proposes “spatiotemporal IDs”: approximately linear location components written into object-token activations at modality-integration layers. Activation swapping and steering across several VLMs provide intriguing evidence that these components influence simple spatial and temporal answers, with preliminary diagnostic and training applications. The core idea is promising, but the supplied manuscript does not adequately support the stronger claims of a general causal mechanism or architectural fault localization.
strengths: A clear and potentially novel mechanistic hypothesis connects visual-to-text information transfer with linear binding representations, supported by complementary swapping, extraction, and intervention experiments (pp. 3–6).
The analysis spans 11 image VLMs and extends to video models, suggesting some cross-family generality rather than a single-model curiosity (pp. 6, 9–10).
The diagnostic and auxiliary-loss applications are useful directions beyond merely identifying a probe-correlated representation (pp. 7–9).
weaknesses: The causal evidence is not sufficiently controlled: steering uses a very large tuned scale (α=5), same-norm noise itself flips 29.5% of beliefs, and the paper lacks direction-matched nulls, specificity tests on unrelated outputs, and dose-response analyses. Thus the reported interventions establish influence but not that spatial IDs are the mechanism mediating ordinary inference (pp. 5–7).

The diagnostic conclusions overreach the measurements. Output sensitivity to pixel masking cannot cleanly distinguish vision-encoder failure from cross-modal integration or downstream nonlinear effects, yet the paper attributes LLaVA and LLaMA failures to specific architectural stages (pp. 7–9).

Evidence for improvement and temporal generality is preliminary: fine-tuning uses one small model with no seeds/error bars and only a same-step control, while the displayed temporal results are noisy and chiefly from one model (pp. 9–10). Moreover, repeatedly cited appendices containing essential implementation details and ablations are absent from the supplied 14 pages.
response.score_rationale: The work has a compelling, interpretable hypothesis and unusually broad initial experiments, placing it near the acceptance boundary. However, high-magnitude interventions with weak null controls, unsupported component-level diagnoses, limited training/video validation, and missing referenced appendices prevent confident acceptance. I therefore assign a marginally-below-acceptance score; uncertainty remains because the absent appendices may contain some needed controls.

response.summary: The paper proposes “spatiotemporal IDs”: approximately linear location components bound to object-token activations in VLMs. Activation swapping, extracted-direction steering, diagnostic analyses, one finetuning experiment, and a video extension provide suggestive evidence for this mechanism. The idea is interesting and potentially useful, but the causal and architectural conclusions exceed what the reported controls establish, and the referenced appendices containing essential details are absent from the supplied manuscript.
strengths: A novel, intuitive hypothesis connects cross-modal information transfer with linear binding mechanisms and yields testable interventions (pp. 3–6).
The study has unusually broad image-model coverage—11 VLMs—and tests interventions on natural images rather than relying solely on synthetic extraction data (pp. 5–6).
The paper explores practical implications through failure analysis, auxiliary spatial supervision, and an analogous temporal mechanism in video models (pp. 7–10).
weaknesses: The strongest causal claim is undercontrolled: steering uses a large tuned scale (α=5), noise itself flips 29.5% of beliefs, and the paper lacks controls such as random directions matched for covariance/selection or interventions outside object tokens. Thus the results support causal relevance of these directions, not that the proposed IDs are the mechanism (pp. 5–7).

Many essential specifications and promised ablations are deferred to Appendices A–E, but no appendices appear in the supplied 14-page manuscript. Sample construction, model-specific layers, statistical uncertainty, extraction robustness, adversarial-ID selection, and finetuning details therefore cannot be assessed (pp. 3–6, 9–10).

Several conclusions are stronger than the evidence: input masking cannot cleanly localize failure to the vision encoder versus cross-modal integration; the theoretical sketch assumes the positional decomposition and attention transfer it seeks to explain; and the single-run, single-model finetuning table lacks seeds/error bars and stronger baselines (pp. 5, 7–9).
response.score_rationale: The core hypothesis and cross-model intervention results are promising and novel enough to approach acceptance. However, missing appendices and insufficient controls leave substantial uncertainty about robustness, causal specificity, and the diagnostic claims. I therefore rate it marginally below acceptance rather than a clear reject.
